description_full: Cabot Corporation operates as a specialty chemicals and performance materials company. It operates through two segments, Reinforcement Materials and Performance Chemicals. The company offers reinforcing carbons that are used in tires as a rubber reinforcing agent and performance additive, as well as in industrial products, such as hoses, belts, extruded profiles, and molded goods; and engineered elastomer composites solutions. It also provides specialty carbons for use in inks, coatings, plastics, adhesives, toners, batteries, and displays; conductive additives and fumed alumina used in lead acid and lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles; fumed silica used in adhesives, sealants, cosmetics, batteries, inks, toners, silicone elastomers, coatings, polishing slurries, and pharmaceuticals; and fumed alumina for use in various products, including inkjet media, lighting, coatings, cosmetics, and polishing slurries. In addition, it offers aerogel, a hydrophobic, silica-based particle to use in various thermal insulation and specialty chemical applications; masterbatch and conductive compound products that are used in automotive, industrial, packaging, infrastructure, agriculture, consumer products, and electronics industries; and inkjet colorants for inkjet printing applications, as well as carbon nanotubes and fumed metal oxides. The company sells its products through distributors and sales representatives in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. Cabot Corporation was founded in 1882 and is headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Cabot Corporation is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $3.8B market cap on $3.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at 17% against a 8% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 21% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $214M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.98× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.4×.

Management returns a meaningful 6.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Elevated short interest (13.4% of float) — sophisticated money is betting the other way
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 17% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Trading at a 35% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
40 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk
Basic Materials sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

sect: Its 13% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (9%).

It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+11.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 222 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 20% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 12% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.91, it moves roughly with the market.
About $28.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The stock trades 35% below its DCF fair value of $115, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 42%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $40.07 to $305 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 4% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 5.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $83.00 on average, 12% above the price.
The price implies 1.2% annual cash-flow growth, 6pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.75).
It runs a 21% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.98x.
ROE of 13% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.4% of revenue on R&D and 0.5% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($254.0M of cash against $1.3B of debt), with interest covered 6.4x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.6% over 3 years, 1.9% over 5 years and 4.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 17.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 28.1% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 5.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 7, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 6.5% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.4%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 6.0% a year to shareholders (3.5% in buybacks and 2.5% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 3.9% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 13.4% of the float, 12.8 days to cover.
people: With about 4,032 employees, each generates about $929K of revenue, 1.5x the Basic Materials median.
That works out to $53K of free cash flow per employee.
